reason: Thousand Words FilmS takes Verne's travellers down Snaefells to a sea under the earth, with a wordless map in place of the runes and a giant blind salamander modelled on the real olm. The 39-minute release explains what was borrowed, what was invented and why the chapter cards name places rather than events.

The sun is not dead but held captive, and a young woman from a frozen northern village must carry the last ember into the wilderness. Sasha Fevralskaya, whose Kagome won Curious Refuge's horror competition, moves from a children's game to folk ritual, made in Higgsfield Cinema Studio for the Talent Contest.

An actress who exists only inside the worlds she was made for finds herself in a Western beside an orc from another genre entirely. Avaren's comedy turns a basic condition of generated film, characters written into whatever scene is asked of them, into the story itself; it was made for the Higgsfield Talent Contest and produced by The Blue Horizon.

Dair Karakeev returns to the survivor and dog of his 51-minute GOOD BOY with a 32-minute first episode: Argos's newborn pups need vaccines, and the search leads Jane to an abandoned research station. Magnific commissioned the sequel, and the release credits a small team for producing, sound and cinematography.

An alien ship over a quiet Japanese city turns out to be on an errand: two visitors have come to collect a vintage car from an old takoyaki seller. Allan Ripley shapes the comedy in the look of 1990s TV anime and names each tool by role, from Seedance 2.5 video to Dehancer colour.
